overview: Deinonychus antirrhopus sparked the Dinosaur Renaissance. John Ostrom's 1969 description overturned a century of thinking about dinosaurs as slow, cold-blooded, tail-dragging reptiles by demonstrating that this Early Cretaceous predator was active, agile and held its tail rigid for balance. The "Velociraptors" in Jurassic Park are modelled directly on Deinonychus — roughly twice the size of an actual Velociraptor.

Multiple Deinonychus specimens found near a Tenontosaurus carcass in Montana generated the still-debated pack-hunting hypothesis. Whether it hunted cooperatively or whether multiple individuals simply fed opportunistically at a carcass is unresolved; the fossil association alone cannot distinguish between the two interpretations.

articles.title: The Dinosaur Renaissance
articles.body: Ostrom's 1969 monograph on Deinonychus is widely cited as the trigger for the Dinosaur Renaissance — the paradigm shift from sluggish reptiles to active, bird-like animals. The paper demonstrated an enlarged sickle claw held raised while walking, long arms adapted for grasping, a stiff tail acting as a dynamic stabiliser, and an overall body plan inconsistent with the cold-blooded, slow-moving model that had prevailed since Owen.

articles.title: Sickle claw and predation
articles.body: The enlarged second-toe claw was held raised off the ground during walking and used to pin and puncture prey during an attack. Functional analysis suggests it was most effective as a restraint and wound-opener rather than a slashing weapon. The strong forelimbs with three large-clawed fingers helped grip struggling prey.

articles.title: Evolutionary significance
articles.body: Ostrom's comparison of Deinonychus with Archaeopteryx — noticing over a dozen skeletal features shared between them — helped re-establish the dinosaurian origin of birds, a hypothesis first proposed by Thomas Henry Huxley in the 1860s but long neglected. Deinonychus became the keystone taxon in the cladistic arguments for birds as living theropod dinosaurs.

record.description: Deinonychus antirrhopus was a medium-sized predatory dromaeosaurid from the Cloverly Formation and equivalent units of North America. Multiple partial skeletons, skull elements, teeth and growth stages document the animal, although many early reconstructions combined several individuals.
facts: The enlarged second-toe claw is directly preserved and was held clear of the ground in walking.
Feathering is strongly supported by close phylogenetic bracketing, even though no direct body-feather impressions are known for Deinonychus.
Co-occurrence of several individuals and Tenontosaurus does not establish coordinated pack hunting.

presentation.heroLead: A lightly built Early Cretaceous dromaeosaurid whose enlarged sickle claw and agile skeleton helped change the picture of dinosaurs from sluggish reptiles to active animals.

heroMedia.title: Life restoration of Deinonychus antirrhopus
heroMedia.alt: Life restoration of a feathered Deinonychus antirrhopus walking in side view, with the second-toe claw raised off the ground
heroMedia.caption: A feathered restoration with proportions based on a published skeletal reconstruction. Feathering is inferred from close relatives rather than preserved on Deinonychus itself; colour and patterning are interpretive.

animalParagraphs: Deinonychus was a mid-sized predatory theropod, roughly three to three and a half metres long and perhaps 60–100 kilograms in mass, with a long stiffened tail, grasping three-fingered hands and a large, strongly curved claw on the second toe of each foot. Its name, 'terrible claw', refers to that weapon, which was held clear of the ground during walking.

The skull was relatively deep with a wide gape and blade-like serrated teeth. Early reconstructions gave it a shorter, more boxy head because they combined bones from more than one individual; later specimens show a longer, lower profile more like other dromaeosaurids. Growth-stage differences in the skull and teeth have also been documented.

No feathers are preserved on any Deinonychus fossil, but feathered relatives on either side of it in the family tree make an extensive feather covering the most likely condition. The claw was probably used for gripping and pinning prey, and several individuals have been found with the plant-eater Tenontosaurus, although this does not demonstrate coordinated pack hunting.
animalHighlights: A large retractable second-toe claw is preserved directly and was the inspiration for the genus name.
Its description by John Ostrom in 1969 was central to the idea of active, bird-like dinosaurs.
Feathers are expected on phylogenetic grounds but have never been found on the animal itself.

lifeCards.label: Feeding
lifeCards.level: Supported by teeth and bite marks
lifeCards.reason: Serrated teeth, grasping hands and the sickle claw indicate predation; shed teeth and bite marks link it to Tenontosaurus carcasses, though whether it hunted or scavenged them is debated.

lifeCards.label: Movement
lifeCards.reason: The hindlimbs and stiffened tail indicate a two-legged animal; suggestions of exceptional speed rest on proportions rather than trackways.

lifeCards.label: Known size
lifeCards.reason: No single complete skeleton is known, so length and mass are reconstructed from several individuals of different sizes.

lifeCards.label: Appearance
lifeCards.reason: Body outline is well constrained by the bones; feathering is predicted from relatives and colour is unknown.

presentation.classificationSummary: Deinonychus is a dromaeosaurid within Eudromaeosauria, the group of larger, robust 'raptors' that also includes Velociraptor, Dromaeosaurus and Utahraptor. Its close relationship to birds within Maniraptora is well supported.

related.reason: Compare with a smaller Asian dromaeosaurid known from articulated skeletons and quill knobs.
Compare with a much larger, heavily built dromaeosaurid from slightly older North American rocks.
The ornithopod repeatedly found alongside Deinonychus remains and teeth.

questions.title: Did it hunt in packs?
questions.copy: Several Deinonychus with one Tenontosaurus is suggestive, but such associations can form without cooperative hunting, and tooth chemistry suggests juveniles and adults ate differently.

questions.title: How was the claw used?
questions.copy: Slashing, stabbing, climbing and pinning prey have all been proposed; mechanical tests favour gripping and restraint, but the question remains open.

questions.title: How extensive was its plumage?
questions.copy: Feathers are inferred from relatives such as Velociraptor and Microraptor. Their distribution, length and colour on Deinonychus are unknown.

review.ageReviewNote: Secure Cloverly occurrences are late Aptian-Albian, broadly 115-108 Ma.

panel.headline: Several partial skeletons and many teeth, but no single complete animal.
panel.standfirst: Deinonychus is known from a handful of partial skeletons collected in Montana and Wyoming since the 1930s, plus skull elements, isolated bones and abundant shed teeth. Together they cover most of the skeleton, though the famous early reconstructions were composites.

coverage.label: Good
coverage.basis: Most skeletal regions are represented across several individuals, including hands, feet and skull elements, but no specimen is complete and some regions are known from few bones.

knownRemains.title: What is actually preserved?
knownRemains.summary: Partial skulls and jaws, vertebrae and the rod-stiffened tail, shoulder and pelvic girdles, forelimbs with complete hands, and hindlimbs with the diagnostic feet, spread across the Yale, Harvard and American Museum collections. Shed teeth are common in the Cloverly Formation and in the Antlers Formation of Oklahoma.
knownRemains.note: Because the material comes from several individuals of different sizes, any single mounted skeleton combines bones from more than one animal.

materialGroups.label: Skull and jaws
materialGroups.value: Partial skulls, braincase, maxillae and dentaries with teeth from several individuals; the first published skull was a composite reconstruction.

materialGroups.label: Vertebral column
materialGroups.value: Cervical, dorsal, sacral and caudal vertebrae, including the long ossified-tendon rods that stiffened the tail.

materialGroups.label: Girdles and limbs
materialGroups.value: Scapulocoracoid, furcula, pelvis, forelimbs with three-fingered hands and hindlimbs with complete feet including the sickle claw.

materialGroups.label: Exceptional preservation
materialGroups.value: Bite marks and shed teeth on Tenontosaurus bones, and eggshell found in association with one specimen; no feathers or skin are known.

specimenCards.title: YPM 5205 · holotype
specimenCards.description: An incomplete skeleton excavated by Yale parties led by John Ostrom in 1964–65 near Bridger, Montana, and described in 1969. It includes the left foot with the enlarged second-toe claw that gives the genus its name.

specimenCards.title: AMNH 3015
specimenCards.description: A partial skeleton collected by Barnum Brown in 1931 and left undescribed for decades under a manuscript name; it became one of the principal referred specimens once Deinonychus was recognised.

interpretation.label: Directly observed
interpretation.value: Partial skeletons of several individuals with the sickle claw, stiffened tail and grasping hands, plus abundant shed teeth and bite marks on Tenontosaurus bones.

interpretation.label: Scientific interpretation
interpretation.value: An active, agile predator whose anatomy supports the dinosaur–bird link; the claw is best explained as a gripping and pinning tool, and feathers are inferred from bracketing relatives.

interpretation.label: Still unknown
interpretation.value: Feather distribution and colour, hunting behaviour, exact adult size and which bones belong to which individual in the early composite reconstructions.
